one_liner: C++ HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket server addon for Node.js, the engine under MoroJS; beat actix-web 1.11-1.14x on a hello-world shootout.
what_it_does: A native Node.js addon (raw V8 bindings, not N-API) that parses HTTP/1.1, runs keep-alive, chunked bodies, WebSocket (optional permessage-deflate) and in-process TLS on Node's own libuv loop. It is not a Node http.Server replacement: the API is serve(callbacks) plus opaque request ids, with onRequest(reqId, methodIdx, path), lazy getters (getHeaders, getQuery, getBody) and one-shot respond(reqId, status, headers, body) or writeHead/write/end streaming. MoroJS uses it as its default transport and falls back to node:http when no prebuilt binary loads; standalone use means writing against this low-level id-based API.
how_it_is_fast: A batched boundary: one JS crossing delivers method index and path, and one corked call sends status, headers and body (the design doc says 2-4 crossings per request against about 10-20 for a general binding), with V8 Fast API call targets on the hot response functions. Fixed replies can skip JS entirely: setStaticRoute and (since 1.1.9) setParamRoute answer inside C++, and prepareResponse builds a header block once for reuse on each request. The warm path avoids allocation (reused per-connection scratch buffers and header strings, a Date header cached once per second, uv_try_write with no write-request allocation, one write for each pipelined batch), multi-core runs as SO_REUSEPORT workers, and release binaries are built with clang -O3 -flto plus PGO. The parser is a scalar, table-driven RFC 9112 parser: the source has no SIMD intrinsics, although DESIGN.md calls it 'SIMD-friendly'.
when_to_use: You already run MoroJS on Node 20-26: this is its default engine, with automatic node:http fallback on unsupported platforms or ABIs.

Node.js HTTP/1.1 services where transport overhead dominates and many responses are fixed or echo one path segment, so static routes, parameter routes and prepared templates can answer without entering JS.

Pipelined HTTP/1.1 clients: the author's run (Apple M2 Ultra, wrk -c100, pipelined x10) shows raw engine 832,171 req/s vs raw uWebSockets.js 652,934; without pipelining the two were 108,446 vs 106,287.
You want native HTTPS/WSS termination plus WebSocket with permessage-deflate in one MIT npm package, with prebuilt binaries for glibc, musl, macOS and Windows x64.
Linux 6.1+ hosts with heavy keep-alive load where you can A/B the opt-in io_uring transport (MORO_ENGINE_TRANSPORT=uring).
when_not_to_use: Choosing a stack on this number alone: the win over actix-web comes from hello-world handlers where GET / and POST /user are engine static routes that never run JS. No data covers handlers that do real work in JS.
Tail-latency-sensitive services at low or medium concurrency: in the same run p99 was 0.72 ms vs actix 0.39 ms at c=64 and 2.42 vs 1.58 ms at c=256. It was lower only at c=512 (3.05 vs 3.22 ms).
You need HTTP/2, HTTP/3, multi-certificate SNI or OCSP stapling. The engine is HTTP/1.1 only; ALPN HTTP/2 is listed as in progress.

Direct internet exposure of the TLS and HTTP parsers without a proxy: no external security audit has been done, and THREAT_MODEL.md says to front it with a proxy or review it first. maxConnections defaults to unlimited.

Risk-averse production use: repo created 2026-07-09, one npm maintainer, 0 stars, 0 issues filed, 723 npm downloads in 30 days, nine releases in 11 weeks. Also not for streaming large uploads: request bodies are buffered in full before onRequest (10 MB default cap).

integration.form: module (npm meta package @morojs/engine with prebuilt .node binaries in per-platform optional packages, one for each Node ABI; source build via tools/build.mjs)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond the per-platform binary package; links the libuv, OpenSSL and zlib inside the host Node binary. Source builds fetch Node headers and a sha-pinned v8-fast-api-calls.h.
integration.min_toolchain: Node.js >= 20 (ABIs 115/127/131/137/141/147 = Node 20/22/23/24/25/26). Source builds: C++20; the release lane uses clang-18 + lld for LTO/PGO, MSVC /std:c++20 on Windows. Minimum compiler version not documented.
integration.platforms: darwin arm64/x64, linux x64/arm64 (glibc and musl), win32 x64. Release x64 binaries target -march=x86-64-v2 (SSE4.2/POPCNT) and arm64 targets armv8.2-a. The io_uring transport needs Linux 6.1+ and is opt-in. SO_REUSEPORT is POSIX-only (ignored on Windows).
integration.thread_safety: Single-threaded per event loop: each thread (main or worker_threads) runs its own servers, request/WebSocket ids never cross threads, and there are no locks. For multi-core, run one engine per worker thread or process with reusePort.

gotchas: Before 1.1.7, callbacks ran outside a Node callback scope. A response sent from a promise continuation could stall for 5-29 s, and under load none such completed. Use >= 1.1.7 and check probe().capabilities.callbackScope.

V8 Fast API targets install only when the running V8 major.minor matches the one the binary was built against. They apply only to Smi ids and sequential one-byte string bodies. Otherwise calls silently take the slower regular path; probe().fastApi reports why.

Static and parameter routes run no JS, so no middleware, logging or auth runs for them. Only an exact method match short-circuits (HEAD against a GET route reaches JS). A parameter segment is sent undecoded ('a%20b' stays 'a%20b').

The io_uring transport falls back to libuv silently under Docker's default seccomp profile, gVisor or kernels before 6.1. The default is still libuv because io_uring used more CPU per request in small-batch cases; check probe().transport.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: In the same 2026-09-24 run, uWebSockets.js (189,157 / 178,265 / 174,621 req/s) was 4-8% behind, fulmine.js (223,508 / 210,337 / 203,996) was 10-12% ahead and Ultimate Express (179,836 / 170,080 / 165,795) was about 10% behind. Pick this engine when you use MoroJS or want its id-based native API with in-process TLS and automatic node:http fallback. Pick fulmine.js for the top raw number, or Ultimate Express if you need Express API compatibility.
verified_claims_summary: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks run of 2026-09-24 (develop f673364): zrk closed loop over keep-alive connections, 15 s per level, with each figure averaged over GET /, GET /user/0 and POST /user. The server was pinned to 4 cores of an undisclosed 16-thread x86_64 Linux host (the CPU name in the data is hard-coded). The raw engine as a Node 26 cluster (^1.1.6, most likely 1.1.7 because the run predates the 1.1.9 publish) did 203,452 / 187,047 / 182,455 req/s at c=64/256/512 against actix-web 4.8 (Rust 1.98, opt-level 3, LTO, codegen-units=1) at 179,203 / 168,270 / 163,415, or 1.14x / 1.11x / 1.12x with both about 99% CPU-saturated. The older-method 2026-09-20 snapshot showed only 1.03-1.05x, and the engine's author submitted the benchmark entry (PR #9801).
status_note: Active: 1.1.9 released 2026-09-24, 45 commits since the repo was created on 2026-07-09. MIT, installable from npm with prebuilt binaries, but young, single-maintainer and not externally audited.
